explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Amos 3:1 says the LORD's word is against the whole family He brought up out of the land of Egypt. He is speaking to the children of Israel. Nice pick.
Assyria is a real place in the Bible, but it's not the one in this verse. Amos 3:1 says the family was brought up out of the land of Egypt. Egypt is the one to remember here.
Babylon is a good Bible name, so I see why it came to mind. But this verse says the whole family was brought up out of the land of Egypt. Hold onto Egypt for this one, friend.

explanations.answer: Punish them for all their iniquities
explanations.explanation: That's right, and it's a heavy one. The LORD says, “Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.” Notice the word 'therefore.' It ties being known by Him to what comes next. This is a serious line, so I'll let it sit for a second.

I get why that sounds like a good fit. But the LORD doesn't say protection here. He says, “Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.” Sometimes the verse says the harder thing, and we have to let it.

That would be a different verse, friend. Here the LORD says, “Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.” Forgiveness isn't what He says in this verse. It's punishment.

explanations.answer: He roars when he has prey
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The question is, “Does a lion roar in the forest when he has no prey?” The answer is built right in: a lion roars when he has prey. Amos asks it again about a young lion: “Does a young lion growl in his den if he has caught nothing?”

explanations.answer: He roars when a storm comes
explanations.explanation: Storms are a fine guess, but they're not in this verse. Amos 3:4 asks if a lion roars in the forest when he has no prey. So the roar goes with prey, not weather.

That's a reasonable guess, but the verse doesn't mention night. It asks whether a lion roars in the forest when he has no prey. And it asks whether a young lion growls in his den if he has caught nothing. Both questions point to prey.

Yes, catch! The text asks, “Does a trap spring from the ground when it has nothing to catch?” No catch, no spring. Right before that, a bird doesn't land in a snare where no bait has been set. Amos keeps stacking up these everyday pictures.

Guard is a clever guess, but it's not the word here. The verse asks if a trap springs from the ground when it has nothing to catch. A trap doesn't stand watch like a doorman, friend. It springs on something.

Traps can be sneaky, so I see where you're coming from. But Amos 3:5 asks, “Does a trap spring from the ground when it has nothing to catch?” The word is catch, not hide. The question is about the trap having something to catch.
Tremble, baker! Amos asks, “If a ram’s horn sounds in a city, do the people not tremble?” When the horn sounds in a city, the people tremble. The answer is built right into the question.
I like the optimism, friend. But the verse asks, “If a ram’s horn sounds in a city, do the people not tremble?” The people tremble, not rejoice. Keep that hopeful spirit for another verse.

Rest would be nice, but a ram's horn is not a lullaby. The verse asks, “If a ram’s horn sounds in a city, do the people not tremble?” The people tremble. I know a few bakers who do the same when my timer goes off.
True! Amos asks, “If calamity comes to a city, has not the LORD caused it?” The question points to the LORD as the One who caused it. That's the point Amos is making as the questions pile up.

This one is true, friend. Amos 3:6 asks, “If calamity comes to a city, has not the LORD caused it?” So the text points to the LORD as the One who caused it. It's a hard line, but it's what the verse says.

Right! The text says, “Surely the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets.” Just after that, the passage says, “The Lord GOD has spoken—who will not prophesy?” (Amos 3:8). So the prophets are the ones He shares His plan with.

Kings are a natural guess, but this verse doesn't name them. It says the Lord GOD reveals His plan to His servants the prophets. Amos is one of those servants, and he's a sheepherder from Tekoa (Amos 1:1). No crown required.

Priests are a reasonable guess, but this verse doesn't mention them. It says the Lord GOD reveals His plan to His servants the prophets. So the answer is the prophets. I get mixed up on titles too, friend.

That's not what the verse says, friend. After the lion roars, the text says, “The Lord GOD has spoken—who will not prophesy?” The question points the opposite way from hearing and staying quiet. So this one is False.

False is right, baker! Amos says, “The Lord GOD has spoken—who will not prophesy?” The verse doesn't say a person could hear Him and stay quiet. It asks who won't prophesy once the Lord GOD has spoken. Good catch.

explanations.answer: The great unrest and acts of oppression
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker! They're told to see the great unrest in the city and the acts of oppression in her midst. Ashdod and Egypt are called to take a look. I think this one hurts.

explanations.answer: The new walls going up around it
explanations.explanation: Walls would be a normal thing to see, but they're not in the verse. The call is to see the great unrest in the city and the acts of oppression in her midst. That's what they're sent to look at. Not a construction site.

explanations.answer: The great feast being held there
explanations.explanation: A feast would be a happier sight, friend. But Amos 3:9 says they're told to see the great unrest in the city and the acts of oppression in her midst. No party in this verse. That's the picture the LORD sets out.
The text says the opposite, friend. The LORD declares, “For they know not how to do right…” So the people of Samaria don't know how to do right. This one is False.
False is right! The LORD declares, “For they know not how to do right…” It's a hard thing to read, and it sets up what comes next. Good eye, baker.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, “They store up violence and destruction in their citadels.” A citadel is a stronghold, and what they've stored up in theirs is not good. I think this one hurts.

Silver and gold sound like normal things to store in a stronghold. But this verse says something else: “They store up violence and destruction in their citadels.” That's what the LORD says is in there. It's a heavy line.

Grain and wine would be a decent pantry, friend. But the LORD says, “They store up violence and destruction in their citadels.” That's what He says they store. It's a very different kind of storeroom.

explanations.answer: An enemy will surround the land
explanations.explanation: Right! The Lord GOD says, “An enemy will surround the land; he will pull down your strongholds and plunder your citadels.” That word 'Therefore' at the start of the verse connects it to what came before. It's a heavy moment, so I'll just say well done.

explanations.answer: A drought will dry up the land
explanations.explanation: A drought is a fair guess, but it's not in this verse. The Lord GOD says, “An enemy will surround the land…” It's an enemy that comes, not dry weather. Good thinking, friend.

explanations.answer: A flood will cover the land
explanations.explanation: I see why a flood came to mind, since Bible bakers know that word. But here the Lord GOD says, “An enemy will surround the land; he will pull down your strongholds and plunder your citadels.” So it's an enemy, not water.

True, baker. The LORD says the Israelites dwelling in Samaria will be rescued having just the corner of a bed or the cushion of a couch. Like a shepherd snatching two legs or a piece of an ear from a lion's mouth. It's a hard picture, so I'll keep it simple.

This one is true, friend. The LORD says that as the shepherd snatches from the mouth of the lion two legs or a piece of an ear, so the Israelites dwelling in Samaria will be rescued having just the corner of a bed or the cushion of a couch. They're rescued with almost nothing. It's a sobering picture.

Jacob, baker! The Lord GOD, the God of Hosts, says, “Hear and testify against the house of Jacob…” (Amos 3:13). That name is the one that fills the blank. The One speaking is the Lord GOD Himself, and the house He names is Jacob's. Well done.
Esau is a good Bible name, and he was Jacob's twin brother (Genesis 25:24-26). But the verse says, “Hear and testify against the house of Jacob…” So the answer is Jacob. I mix up twins too, friend.

Pharaoh was Egypt's king in the days of Moses (Exodus 5:1), so I see the link with Egypt earlier in the passage. But this verse says to hear and testify against the house of Jacob. Pharaoh isn't named here. That's the Jacob one, friend.

explanations.answer: They'll be cut off and fall to the ground
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker! The LORD says, “the horns of the altar will be cut off, and they will fall to the ground.” It's all part of the day He punishes Israel for their transgressions. A very serious day.

explanations.answer: They'll be covered in fresh gold again
explanations.explanation: That would be a shiny ending, but it's not what the verse says. The LORD says, “the horns of the altar will be cut off, and they will fall to the ground.” So no fresh gold. Just cut off and down.

explanations.answer: They'll be carried off to the land of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt did show up earlier in the passage, so I get the pull. But this verse says, “the horns of the altar will be cut off, and they will fall to the ground.” The horns fall to the ground, not off to Egypt.
Not quite, friend. The LORD says, “I will tear down the winter house along with the summer house…” So both come down, not just the winter one. This is a False.

False is right, baker! The LORD says, “I will tear down the winter house along with the summer house; the houses of ivory will also perish, and the great houses will come to an end…” Neither house is left standing. Nice catch on that little detail.
